tagline: Military-road heritage and a New Deal campground among Wisconsin's pines and hemlocks.
intro: Heritage Drive passes through hardwoods, giant hemlocks and pines in the Chequamegon-Nicolet National Forest. The Federal Highway Administration gives this Wisconsin drive a length of 15 miles and recommends two to three hours to tour it. Its National Forest Scenic Byway designation covers parts of Military Road and Butternut Lake Road, honoring the route’s heritage.

Military Road followed the Old Superior Trail, used for trade by the Ojibwa, Menominee and Winnebago. Trappers, mail carriers and livestock dealers joined that traffic, supplying northern Michigan’s copper mines and settlements. After the timber ran out, logging companies sold land for farms and homesteads. Many farms were abandoned; federal land purchases began in 1928, followed by the establishment of the Nicolet National Forest in 1933. Later, historian and naturalist Walt Goldsworthy campaigned for special recognition of Military Road. A 1992 newspaper editorial preserved by the Three Lakes Museum records his recognition at the byway’s dedication.

From Highway 70 east of Eagle River, the approach to Franklin Lake turns south onto Military Road, then east onto Butternut Lake Road. At the lake, historic stone and log buildings stand among mature pines and hemlocks. The Franklin Nature Trail continues through forest to a view of Butternut Lake and a boardwalk across a bog.

moments.title: Military Road
moments.text: Creek names preserve a distance system along Military Road: Fourmile Creek, Seven Mile Creek and Ninemile Creek mark distances from Virgin Lake. By 1920, sections of the road had entered Wisconsin’s state highway system. The Three Lakes section follows its original route. Logging companies sold land along the road after the timber ran out. Immigrants bought cutover land for farms and homesteads, but many farms were abandoned. The soil had proved better suited to growing trees. Federal purchases of abandoned and tax-delinquent land began in 1928; the Nicolet National Forest was established in 1933.

moments.title: Franklin Lake
moments.text: Stone and log structures built by the Civilian Conservation Corps are scattered through Franklin Lake Campground. The first layout was staked by three men on snowshoes during the winter of 1935 and 1936. The campground took shape in 1936 through the work of the Corps and the Works Progress Administration, and opened in 1937 with 12 campsites. It entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1988. Two historic log picnic pavilions built by the Corps remain part of the recreation area. The setting includes mature pine and hemlock trees and a sandy beach beside the lake.
moments.notice: Look for the campground’s historic stone and log structures.

moments.title: Franklin Nature Trail
moments.text: The Franklin Nature Trail passes through northern hardwood, pine and hemlock forest, including trees more than 400 years old. A view of Butternut Lake opens from beneath large hemlocks, and a boardwalk crosses a bog where its plants can be seen close up. The short loop at the trail’s beginning accommodates wheelchair users. In spring, wildflowers bloom along this route through the forest and wetland. For a longer excursion, the Hidden Lake Trail branches off midway, loops south of Butternut Lake past Luna-White Deer Campground, and returns to Franklin Lake Campground.
moments.notice: The bog boardwalk brings its plants close to the trail.
